tapeLine: Stocks closed a choppy, triple-witching Friday little changed: the S&P 500 added 0.17% to 7,650.50 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.39% to 26,522.55, while the Dow slipped 95.40 points (-0.18%) to 51,682.64, capping a losing week for the Dow (-1.7%, its worst since March) and the S&P 500 (-0.1%), with only the Nasdaq higher on the week (+0.7%), per Yahoo Finance's and TheStreet's Friday market wraps. Overnight Saturday, Houthi forces fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh for the first time and struck an Aramco facility at Yanbu on the Red Sea; Saudi air defenses said they intercepted the Riyadh missile and gave no confirmation of damage at Yanbu, per Al Jazeera. Oil fell anyway: Brent crude futures dropped 1.71% to $102.09 a barrel and WTI fell 1.96% to $98.33 Monday morning as traders focused on Saudi export flows holding near 4 million bpd rather than the attack itself, per CNBC. US stock futures rose Monday on the retreating oil and softer yields — Dow futures +0.8%, S&P 500 futures +0.7%, Nasdaq-100 futures +1.1% — with markets also looking ahead to Thursday's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, per Bloomberg's Sunday-evening wrap. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee speaks at 6:30 ET and the Chicago Fed National Activity Index (Aug) is due at 7:30 ET; the week's bigger catalysts are Wednesday's flash PMIs and Thursday's summit.
matters:
Friday closed a choppy, triple-witching session little changed: the S&P 500 added 0.17% to 7,650.50 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.39% to 26,522.55, while the Dow slipped 95.40 points (-0.18%) to 51,682.64, per Yahoo Finance's and TheStreet's Friday market wraps. The week itself was a loser for two of three major indexes — the Dow fell 1.7%, its worst week since March, and the S&P 500 slipped 0.1%, while only the Nasdaq gained (+0.7%) — as markets digested Wednesday's Fed hike and the mixed data that followed it.

Saturday brought the sharpest escalation yet in the Saudi conflict this brief has tracked since 10 September: Houthi forces fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh itself for the first time and separately struck an Aramco facility at Yanbu on the Red Sea. Saudi air defenses said the Riyadh missile was intercepted; officials gave no confirmation of damage at Yanbu, per Al Jazeera. Oil fell anyway on Monday — Brent dropped 1.71% to $102.09 and WTI fell 1.96% to $98.33 — as traders weighed Saudi export flows holding near 4 million barrels a day against the attack itself, per CNBC.

Correcting Friday's framing: the 18 September brief described the Houthi advance as "reigniting Yemen's civil war" on a track "separate from the East-West pipeline itself." That undersold the story. The Houthis are an Iran-aligned belligerent in the wider 2026 Iran war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on 28 February and has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed since — Hormuz traffic was still down roughly 95% from pre-war levels as of late August, per Al Jazeera's reporting. The East-West pipeline, Saudi Arabia's overland bypass to the Red Sea, has itself been down since drone strikes on 11 September. Saturday's strike on Riyadh means Saudi Arabia is now exposed on both of its export corridors from the same war, not two unrelated disputes.

The Fed's second-hike question stayed genuinely open. The September dot plot showed 16 of 18 FOMC participants penciling in at least one more 2026 hike, with four seeing room for two; fed funds futures priced roughly an 87% chance of at least one more 25bp move by the December meeting, per reporting on the SEP. No new data has arrived since Thursday's mixed jobless-claims/housing prints to move that further; Wednesday's flash PMIs are the next scheduled test.

The Trump-Xi summit, set for Thursday in Washington, is now the week's largest scheduled catalyst: a tariff-truce extension (the 2025 Busan truce expires in November), rare earths, Taiwan and AI governance are all on the agenda, and Big Tech CEOs are set to join a related White House session on AI rules the same day, per The National and Seoul Economic Daily. The AI-China thread stayed on its separate, political track over the weekend: China's Foreign Ministry and state media rejected Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's 14 September call to tighten chip export controls and slow frontier AI development, calling it a "Cold War playbook," but there has been no crossover into the rate or markets story.

The financing thread stayed open for a further session: no new debt-financed sponsor buyout has printed since Sequence Holdings/DFO's Baldwin Group deal on 14 September, and the weekend produced no new candidate.

Invalidation: Thursday's Trump-Xi summit could move markets well ahead of Wednesday's PMI data if tariffs, Taiwan or AI governance produce a surprise. Saturday's strike on Riyadh is also an untested step-change in the war; Monday's oil move assumes Saudi export data holds up, and that assumption has not yet been tested by a full week of shipping data.

regime.tag: Futures rally on falling oil and firming Fed hike odds; Saudi war risk now hitting Riyadh directly; Trump-Xi summit Thursday is the week's swing factor
regime.sizing: Monday's futures strength (Dow +0.8%, S&P 500 +0.7%, Nasdaq-100 +1.1%) rests on oil's retreat, which itself rests on Saudi export flows holding despite Saturday's first-ever Houthi strike on Riyadh — an assumption not yet tested by a full week of shipping data. The Fed's second-hike odds have firmed to roughly 87% per futures pricing on the September dot plot, but no new economic data has arrived since Thursday to confirm it either way; Wednesday's flash PMIs are the next test. Thursday's Trump-Xi summit is the week's largest scheduled catalyst and could move markets on tariffs, Taiwan or AI governance well ahead of any of the above.

secondOrder: Five threads run into the week. The oil/Iran-war thread escalated over the weekend to its sharpest point yet — the first Houthi strike on Riyadh itself — yet Monday's price action (Brent's fourth drop in five sessions) says the market is pricing continuity of Saudi exports, not disruption; that bet is untested by a full week of shipping data and sits on top of an already-closed Strait of Hormuz and an already-down East-West pipeline, a fact Friday's brief undersold by treating the Houthi advance as a separate, reignited civil war rather than part of the same Iran war. The Fed thread firmed numerically (87% odds of at least one more hike per futures pricing on the dot plot) without any new data to test it; Wednesday's flash PMIs are the next real input. The Trump-Xi thread gained a hard date and a concrete agenda (tariffs, rare earths, Taiwan, AI) for Thursday, making it the week's single largest scheduled catalyst, while the Amodei-China AI dispute stayed adjacent to it but has not crossed into the rate or markets story. And the financing thread stayed open for a further session, with no debt-financed buyout since Baldwin on 14 September.

scorecard.text: The 18 September brief described the Houthi advance on Saudi Arabia as "reigniting Yemen's civil war" on a track "separate from the East-West pipeline itself." That undersold the story: the Houthis are an Iran-aligned belligerent in the wider 2026 Iran war (US/Israeli strikes began 28 February), the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since then, and the East-West pipeline has been down since 11 September drone strikes — all one conflict. Saturday's first-ever Houthi strike on Riyadh itself confirmed it is the same war escalating, not a separate track.

The 18 September brief called Friday a "quadruple-witching" Friday, citing a TradeStation dates page. Friday-of coverage from CNBC and TheStreet instead described it as a "triple witching" session; single-stock futures, the fourth leg of a true quadruple witching, do not trade on major US exchanges.

The 18 September brief left the dot plot's second-2026-hike call unresolved pending more data. It is still unresolved: the September dot plot shows 16 of 18 officials expecting at least one more hike and futures now price roughly 87% odds of one by December, but no new economic data has landed since Thursday to test that pricing. Wednesday's flash PMIs are the next input.

The financing test flagged since 10 September — a large, freshly debt-financed sponsor buyout printing — is still open. No new candidate has surfaced since Sequence Holdings/DFO's Baldwin Group deal on 14 September, and the weekend produced nothing new.

The 15-18 September briefs treated the Amodei/China AI-slowdown dispute as running on a track separate from the Fed-rates story. That held over the weekend: China's rejection of Amodei's export-control push and the run-up to Thursday's Trump-Xi summit stayed on the diplomatic/AI-governance track, with no crossover into rates or the broader tape.
